blocks.text: **The problem.** Given the `root` of a binary tree, return its **top view**: the nodes you would see looking **down** on the tree from above, from the leftmost column to the rightmost. Give the root column 0; a left child is one column to the **left** (−1), a right child one column to the **right** (+1). In each column you see only the **highest** node. (If two nodes share a column and a level, the one further left in level order counts.)

blocks.alt: The tree 1, 2, 3, null, 4, null, null, null, 5, null, 6 with columns marked. 2 is in column -1, 1 and 4 in column 0, 3 and 5 in column 1, 6 in column 2. Looking down from above, column -1 shows 2, column 0 shows 1, column 1 shows 3 and column 2 shows 6. The top view is 2, 1, 3, 6. Nodes 4 and 5 are hidden under 1 and 3.

blocks.code:
Input:  root = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]                         Output: [4, 2, 1, 3, 7]
Input:  root = [1, 2, 3, null, 4, null, null, null, 5, null, 6] Output: [2, 1, 3, 6]

blocks.text: Each node gets two coordinates: its **column** (from the left/right moves) and its **depth**. The top view is, for each column, the node with the **smallest depth**. The approaches differ in how they find "smallest depth per column" and how they put the columns in order.
1. Brute force: record everything, sort, take the first of each column
Walk the tree and record (column, depth, visit order, value) for **every** node. Sort by column, then depth, then visit order, and keep the first entry of each column.
**Time O(n log n)** for the sort, **space O(n)** — everything is recorded, though only one node per column is wanted.
2. Optimal: keep only the highest node per column

Instead of recording everything, keep a map from **column** to the **highest node seen so far** in it. While walking, replace a column's entry only if the new node is **strictly higher** (smaller depth). Preorder visits the left side first, so on a tie the leftmost node is already there. At the end, read the columns in order.

**Time O(n log c)** for c columns (the sorted map or the final sort), **space O(c + h)**. The depth comparisons are needed because depth-first search can reach a deep node in a column **before** a higher one.
3. Best solution: breadth-first, the first node in each column wins

Breadth-first search visits nodes **top to bottom, left to right**. So the **first** node it meets in a column is automatically the highest (and leftmost on a tie) — no depth to compare. And columns form one unbroken range from `minCol` to `maxCol`, so track those two numbers and read the answer column by column — no sorting.

blocks.alt: Breadth-first order on the example: 1 (column 0), 2 (column -1), 3 (column 1), 4 (column 0, already taken), 5 (column 1, already taken), 6 (column 2). The first visitor of each column is kept.

blocks.caption: The caption under each node is its column; hidden nodes are greyed out.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n)** for the queue and the map — no sorting and no depth bookkeeping. Why are the columns an unbroken range? A node in column c is reached through a parent in column c − 1 or c + 1, so columns spread outward one step at a time from 0.

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n log n) time, O(n) space. Optimal: O(n log c) time, O(c + h) space. Best: O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: **Hidden nodes** — a node that zig-zags back under the root (left then right) is in column 0 and hidden.
**A long left arm** — `[1, 2, null, 3, null, 4]`: every node is visible: `[4, 3, 2, 1]`.
**Same column, same level** — the leftmost (first in level order) wins; BFS gets this for free.
**Bottom View** — the **last** node BFS meets in each column: overwrite instead of keeping the first.
**Vertical Order Traversal** — every node of each column, top to bottom (with ties sorted by value on LeetCode 987).
**Vertical Sum** — add up each column instead of keeping one node.
**Left View / Right Side View** — the same idea per **level** instead of per column (previous lesson).
